talk: Profit is the scoreline and cash is your fitness. You can be winning on the P&L and still collapse because the bank account is empty. Clubs rarely die from losses, they die from running out of cash.

terms.meaning: Money actually in the bank right now.
Spreading a big upfront cost across the years it helps you.
How long your cash lasts at the current burn (the cash you lose each month).

questions.prompt: You sign a striker for a $10M fee on a 5-year contract, paid up front. How much of the fee hits THIS year's P&L?
questions.hint: The cost is spread over the contract.
working: The fee is spread over the 5 years the player helps you. That's amortization.
whyNot: Paying up front doesn't make the cost disappear from the P&L. Each of the 5 years takes its share of $2M.
$10M / 2 = $5M spreads it over 2 years. The contract is 5 years, so it's $2M a year.
$10M is the cash that leaves the bank. The P&L spreads the cost over the 5 years of the contract.

questions.prompt: How much cash leaves the bank this year?
working: The P&L says $2M. The bank says $10M. Both are true.
whyNot: The money has gone. Paid up front means all $10M left the bank this year.
$2M is the P&L charge. Cash doesn't care how accountants spread the cost. The full fee was paid today.
That's half the fee, as if you paid in two parts. This fee was paid up front, all $10M.

questions.prompt: You have $6M in the bank and burn $500K a month. How many months of runway do you have?
working: That's the number that tells you when you need to raise money or start winning.
whyNot: 24 months would need 24 x $500K = $12M. Double what you have.
18 months would need 18 x $500K = $9M in the bank. You have $6M.
After 6 months you've only burned 6 x $500K = $3M. Half your cash is still there.

penalty.prompt: The club has {cash} in the bank and burns {burn} a month. How many months of runway?

traps.why: That's years. The question asks for months.

call.title: Paying for the new striker
call.prompt: You've agreed to sign a striker for $1.2M. The selling club will take it all now, or $400,000 now and the rest over two years. Separately, the stadium roof needs $900,000 of repairs in 3 matchdays.

options.label: Pay $1.2M up front
options.result: Profit looks the same either way, but paying it all now leaves too little for the $900,000 roof.

later.text: The roof bill lands and cash is tight. An emergency loan costs $60,000 in fees.

options.label: Pay $400,000 now, the rest later
options.result: Good call. Same player, same profit, but $1.2M - $400,000 = $800,000 stays in the bank, so the roof gets paid without a loan.

later.text: The roof gets fixed, paid from cash. No drama.

options.label: Pay $1.2M now and put off the roof
options.result: A leaking roof costs you fans.

later.text: The roof leaks onto the main stand. 500 fans move elsewhere.

takeaway: Profit is spread over years. Cash is what's in the bank today.
